newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba seeks slower, sustained growth amid cash squeeze. [CORRECTED 13:20 GMT 26/12]
newsitem.headline: Cuba seeks slower, sustained growth amid cash squeeze. [CORRECTED 13:20 GMT 26/12]

text.p: Cuba Tuesday (Corrects day) reported higher than expected economic growth in 1996 but said it aimed for a slower rate of recovery next year as it sought a sustainable level of growth and tries to rein in its trade deficit.

Economy Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez told parliament Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth in 1996 would be 7.8 percent, better than a forecast 5 percent and above last year's 2.5 percent growth, despite what he called exceptionally difficult conditions.

The minister, speaking at the start of a two-day session of the National Assembly, said the 1997 economic plan foresaw GDP growth of 4 percent to 5 percent. The main goal of the plan would be to achieve an improved balance of payments as the basis for sustainable development, he said, without giving figures.
Cuba 's largely state-controlled economy is emerging from sharp contraction of more than 35 percent between 1989 and 1993, triggered by the collapse of the former Soviet Union.
Rodriquez said that Cuba had "crossed the threshold of recovery" this year and was now in a position to "regulate our growth in a planned way".
But he stressed the main limitation was the country's "external financial situation", noting Cuba is critically reliant on expensive short-term credits to cover shortages of foreign exchange.
He called for more efficiency in oil use, a major part of the import bill, and for greater control of investments and of enterprises that operate in the foreign exchange sector.

Exports grew by some 33 percent in 1996, while imports were up 33.3 percent, he said, over the targeted figures of 20 and 15 percent respectively. Next year exports would grow 12 percent, while imports would rise 11.5 percent, he said.

Rodriguez did not give trade figures, other than the percentage rises. But the national bank reported earlier this year that exports in 1995 were worth some $1.45 billion and imports $2.78 billion, for a trade deficit of some $1.3 billion billion. Rodriguez said the trade deficit had risen in 1996 but gave no figure.

The rate of recovery of key exports sugar and nickel is expected to slow somewhat in 1997. The island produced 4.45 million metric tons of sugar in its 1995-96 harvest, and is expected to post another "discreet" improvement in the just-started harvest. In nickel, where 1996 production will be some 55,800 tons, Rodriquez said growth next year would be 20 percent, or an increase of around 11,000 tons.
Tourism, which along with remittances from Cubans abroad, helps offset the trade deficit, was expected to continue to grow.

The minister said economic growth achieved in 1996 was extraordinary, given difficulties faced this year, which included the toughtening of the longstanding U.S. economic embargo in March and a hurricane that damaged crops and buildings in October. These were in addition to higher prices for imports such as food and oil, and lower prices for exports such as sugar and nickel.

Rodriguez said the state budget deficit in 1996 was down to just 2.4 percent of GDP compared with 3.6 percent of GDP in 1995. Finance Minister Manuel Millares, outlining the draft budget for next year, said the deficit would be further trimmed to just two percent of GDP.
Despite the new U.S. Helms-Burton law, which aims to discourage foreign investment in Cuba, Rodriquez noted there were now 260 joint ventures on the island, compared with 212 at the close of 1995.
